title: What is tiered storage (KIP-405), and what problem does it solve?
shortTitle: What is tiered storage (KIP-405), and what problem does it solve?

s1_definition.profdef: Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older, closed segments to cheaper remote storage such as Amazon S3, while they still appear as part of the same topic. This decouples storage from compute, so you can retain data for months or years without buying huge local disks, and it makes brokers faster to scale and recover because they hold far less local data. Consumers reading old offsets transparently fetch from the remote tier.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps this month's transaction ledgers on the clerk's desk for instant access, but moves last year's ledgers to a cheap off-site warehouse. The ledgers are still part of the official records and anyone can request an old one, it just comes from the warehouse instead of the desk. The desk stays small and tidy, the bank keeps seven years of history cheaply, and a new clerk can start work immediately because the desk has very little on it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Tiered storage keeps hot recent segments on local disk and offloads cold segments to cheap remote object storage, so Kafka retains data for years cheaply and brokers scale and recover fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older, closed segments to cheaper remote storage such as Amazon S3, while they still appear as part of the same topic. This decouples storage from compute, so you can retain data for months or years without buying huge local disks, and it makes brokers faster to scale and recover because they hold far less local data. Consumers reading old offsets transparently fetch from the remote tier.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps this month's transaction ledgers on the clerk's desk for instant access, but moves last year's ledgers to a cheap off-site warehouse. The ledgers are still part of the official records and anyone can request an old one, it just comes from the warehouse instead of the desk. The desk stays small and tidy, the bank keeps seven years of history cheaply, and a new clerk can start work immediately because the desk has very little on it.

**One line to remember:** Tiered storage keeps hot recent segments on local disk and offloads cold segments to cheap remote object storage, so Kafka retains data for years cheaply and brokers scale and recover fast.

sections.s2_technical:
A Kafka partition is stored as a sequence of log segment files on a broker's local disk. Traditionally, every byte you retain lives on that local disk, so if you want ninety days of retention for a high-volume topic, you must provision and pay for a lot of fast local disk on every broker, and that disk is coupled to the compute. This coupling is the core problem tiered storage attacks.

With tiered storage enabled, a broker keeps only the most recent segments locally, controlled by a local retention setting, and once a segment is closed and older than the local retention, it is uploaded to the configured remote store and removed from local disk, subject to the overall remote retention. You enable it per topic with configs like `remote.storage.enable=true`, and you set `local.retention.ms` or `local.retention.bytes` for how much stays local while `retention.ms` governs the total including remote. For example, you might keep one day locally and one year in S3.

The remote store is pluggable through a RemoteStorageManager interface, with implementations for object stores like S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob. The broker tracks which segments live remotely in remote log metadata. When a consumer requests an offset that is only in the remote tier, the broker fetches that segment from the remote store and serves it, so from the consumer's point of view nothing changes; it is the same topic and the same offsets, just a slightly higher latency for very old data.

The problems this solves are several. First, cost: object storage is far cheaper per gigabyte than fast local disk, so long retention becomes affordable. Second, elasticity: because brokers hold far less local data, adding or removing a broker and rebalancing partitions moves much less data, so scaling is faster and cheaper. Third, recovery: when a broker fails and a replica must catch up, it has less local data to replicate, so recovery is faster. Fourth, retention flexibility: you can keep data for compliance or reprocessing for months or years without sizing local disks for the worst case.

A senior nuance is the latency tradeoff. Reads of recent data stay fast from local disk, but reads of very old data pay the remote fetch latency, so tiered storage suits workloads where most reads are recent and only occasional backfills or audits touch old data. Another nuance is that the remote store becomes part of your durability and security surface, so you encrypt it, control access with policies, and account for remote-store availability. A final nuance is that tiered storage matured across Kafka versions and is production-ready in recent releases, and some managed Kafka offerings provide it transparently.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must retain transaction event history for seven years to satisfy regulators, but the live analytics and fraud systems almost always read only the last few days. Keeping seven years on local broker disk would be enormously expensive and would make brokers slow to scale and recover.

Problem 1 — seven years of high-volume transaction data on local disks costs a fortune and forces huge brokers. This is exactly what tiered storage solves by offloading old segments to cheap object storage.

Problem 2 — when traffic spikes, adding a broker and rebalancing takes hours because each broker holds terabytes locally. This is exactly what tiered storage solves by keeping local data small so rebalancing moves little.

Problem 3 — an auditor occasionally requests transactions from three years ago, which must still be readable through the same topic. This is exactly what tiered storage provides: old offsets are fetched transparently from the remote tier.

The code will model a tiered-retention planner that, given a message's age, decides whether it is served from local disk or remote storage, and computes local versus remote footprint to show the cost benefit, logged for Rajesh's and Priya's transaction history.

```yaml
# application.yml  (topic-level tiered storage config, applied via CLI)
# kafka-configs --alter --topic transactions --add-config \

  tiered:
    local-retention-days: 1
    total-retention-days: 2555     # ~7 years
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the tiered retention demo
java -cp target/tiered-storage-service-1.0.0.jar \
  com.bank.tiered.TieredStorageDemo

# Enable tiered storage on the topic
kafka-configs --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --alter --topic transactions \
  --add-config remote.storage.enable=true,local.retention.ms=86400000,retention.ms=220752000000
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: reads of transaction records of various ages, and a daily ingest of five hundred gigabytes.

Step 1 — Rajesh's swipe from two hours ago is younger than the one-day local retention, so the planner says it is served from local disk, fast and hot.

Step 2 — Priya's rent credit from five days ago is older than local retention but within the seven-year total, so it was already uploaded to remote object storage and is served from there, slightly slower but transparent.

Step 3 — the auditor's request for a transaction three years ago is also within the seven-year window, so it is fetched from remote storage as the same topic and offset, satisfying the audit.

Step 4 — a record from eight years ago is beyond the total retention, so it has been deleted everywhere and is reported as expired.

Step 5 — the footprint calculation shows that with one day local, the brokers only need about five hundred gigabytes of fast local disk, while roughly one and a quarter petabytes of cold history lives cheaply in object storage, demonstrating the cost benefit.

```
2026-10-24 22:40:01 [INFO] Rajesh recent swipe (age 0d) → LOCAL DISK (fast, hot)
2026-10-24 22:40:01 [INFO] Priya last-week rent credit (age 5d) → REMOTE STORAGE (S3, cold, cheap)
2026-10-24 22:40:01 [INFO] Auditor request (3 years ago) (age 1095d) → REMOTE STORAGE (S3, cold, cheap)
2026-10-24 22:40:01 [INFO] Beyond retention (8 years ago) (age 2920d) → EXPIRED (beyond total retention, deleted)
2026-10-24 22:40:01 [INFO] Local disk needed: 500 GB (hot) vs remote: 1277000 GB (cold, cheap)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer writes transaction events
    │
    ▼
  Broker local disk (hot segments)
    │  active + recent closed segments (< local.retention = 1 day)
    │
    │  segment closes AND age > local.retention
    ▼
  Upload closed segment → Remote Store (S3)  [RemoteStorageManager]
    │  broker removes it from local disk
    │  remote log metadata tracks location
    ▼
  ┌───────────────── Read path ─────────────────┐
  │ consumer requests offset                      │
  │   age <= 1 day  → serve from LOCAL disk (fast)│
  │   1 day < age <= 7 yr → fetch from S3 (cold)  │
  │   age > 7 yr    → EXPIRED (gone)              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Benefit: local disk tiny (fast scale/recover), 7-yr history cheap in S3
```

```
  [ACTIVE local] ─close─→ [CLOSED local] ─age>local.ret─→ [UPLOADED remote]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older closed segments to cheaper remote object storage such as S3, while they remain part of the same topic. A local retention setting controls how much stays on local disk, and the overall retention governs the total including the remote tier, so you might keep one day locally and seven years in object storage.

The core problem it solves is that traditionally every retained byte lived on fast, expensive local disk coupled to the broker's compute. Tiered storage decouples storage from compute, which gives four big wins. It makes long retention affordable because object storage is far cheaper per gigabyte. It makes scaling elastic because brokers hold far less local data, so rebalancing moves much less. It makes recovery faster because a catching-up replica has less to copy. And it gives retention flexibility so you can keep years of data for compliance or reprocessing without sizing local disks for the worst case.

From a consumer's point of view nothing changes, because the broker fetches old segments from the remote store transparently, serving the same topic and the same offsets, just with a little more latency for very old data. The tradeoffs I keep in mind are that remote reads are slower, so it suits workloads where most reads are recent, and that the remote store becomes part of my durability and security surface, so I encrypt it and lock down access.

In my National Bank of India project, regulators required seven years of transaction history, but the fraud and analytics systems almost always read only the last few days. Keeping seven years on local disk would have been enormously expensive and would have made brokers slow to scale. We enabled tiered storage with one day local and seven years in S3, so the brokers stayed small and fast, we scaled out quickly during surges, and an auditor could still pull a three-year-old transaction through the same topic.
